Subject: Follow-up: SLO targets & constraints (post-demo)

Hey Rafael / Monica —

Thanks again for the demo today. Super helpful. As promised, attaching a short doc with the SLOs we need to validate so your team can propose a concrete plan and timing. High-level ask from our side: we need an apples-to-apples comparison vs our current provider across end-to-end p95/p99 for the full feature (client-to-server-to-client), not just model decode time. Our current rough targets are:

- p95 end-to-end <= 250 ms
- p99 end-to-end <= 800 ms
- Sustained throughput: ~300 req/s for our 10-minute busy windows (text generation, average 350 tokens)
- Burst concurrency: up to 1,200 concurrent open streams during launches (SSE/HTTP2 streaming)
- Streaming requirements: per-token tail latency <= 40 ms once streaming starts; ability to sustain 150 concurrent streaming connections per GPU node

We also care about: connection churn (clients opening/closing streams), graceful fallback when capacity constrained, and seeing identical query traces so we can validate request-by-request.

Please include: proposed test plan, required instrumentation changes on our side (headers, sampling), and a timeline for a measurement run. We need recommendations on which hosted config to try first (batching settings, cache warmup, quantization variant if relevant).

Attachments: ACME-SLOs-REQ.pdf

Thanks — looking to kick off as soon as next week if possible.

—Ava

Ava / Ben —

Great notes, thank you. Quick recap and proposed concrete plan below (so we have a single source of truth):

Recap of ACME targets (we heard):
- p95 end-to-end target: <= 250 ms
- p99 end-to-end target: <= 800 ms
- Sustained throughput target: 300 req/s during 10-min windows
- Burst concurrency: up to 1,200 concurrent streaming connections
- Streaming per-token tail: <= 40 ms once stream has started

Assumptions / clarifying Qs (please flag if any are incorrect):
- "End-to-end" means from your client HTTP request entering the edge LB through response bytes arriving back at the client (includes network hop from our edge to model-serving node).
- Sample payloads will be ~350 tokens on average, with a 95th token length of ~1,100 tokens for longer requests.

Proposed measurement plan (what we'll run):
1) Canary A/B run (2 x 30-minute windows)
   - 30 minutes on current provider (your production-like traffic replayed) vs 30 minutes on Redwood hosted config (same traffic replay).
   - We'll use a replay harness you provide + a small traffic faker to simulate connection churn.
2) Metrics & tracing
   - Instrumentation: please add X-Request-Id header (or keep your existing trace id header); we will also set X-Test-Run: ACME-Redwood-202608 to mark traffic.
   - We'll capture request-level timing: edge ingress, route-to-model, model-decode, first-byte-to-client, last-byte.
3) Configs to try for Redwood hosted (order of preference):
   - Config A (low-latency): batching disabled, KV prefix cache warmed, token streaming enabled, quantization: fp16, concurrency cap per node 150, autoscale min nodes = 4
   - Config B (cost-balanced): continuous batching enabled (target batch size 8), token streaming enabled with 20ms chunking, quantization: int8, concurrency cap per node 250, autoscale policy target CPU 70%
4) Success criteria
   - p95 and p99 measured across the full trace (client->client) as stated above; Redwood must show a path to meet p95 by tuning (expected for Config A).
   - For p99 we will highlight tail causes (cold cache, jitter) and propose mitigations (sticky routing, pre-warm).
5) Deliverables
   - Runbook after each 30-min window with raw traces (sampled), aggregated p95/p99, per-route breakdown, and recommended next change.

Timing proposal:
- Kickoff / instrumentation handoff: Tue 2026-08-31
- Replay runs: Wed 2026-09-01 (AM/PM slot)
- Results + recommendations: Thu 2026-09-02

High-level notes on differences vs "current provider":
- We'll show both absolute numbers and a per-request comparison for the same request ids; this will surface whether the tail is model-related or infra/network.
- For streaming, our hosted runtime exposes configurable chunk sizes and a streaming queue which helps tail jitter in many cases; we'll include a streaming-focused run to validate token-tail latency.

Attachments: redwood-measurement-plan.xlsx

Ava — quick technical follow-up from the infra side: a few implementation notes so the measurement is meaningful and we don't hit configuration mismatches mid-run.

1) Streaming concurrency model
- Our hosted runtime supports long-lived streaming (SSE/HTTP2) and we size GPU concurrency differently for streaming vs non-streaming. For the initial trial we recommend a per-node streaming concurrency cap of 150, with autoscale able to add nodes if the aggregate queue grows beyond 2x steady-state.

2) Chunking & buffering
- We'll test two chunk sizes: 20ms (Config B suggestion) and 40ms (Config A fallback). Smaller chunks reduce tail for interactive apps but increase packet overhead; we'll measure client-side tail impacts.

3) Prefix/KV cache warmup
- If you can provide a small warmup window (a 5-minute replay of common prefixes) before the main 30-minute run, we can avoid cold-cache p99 spikes. Please mark warmup traces with X-Test-Run: ACME-WARMUP.

4) Instrumentation hooks we need from your side (minimal):
- Propagate trace id in X-Request-Id
- Include a header X-Client-Conn-Id to help map open streaming connections

I'll join the kickoff and will be the primary Red contact for tuning during the run. If we see p99 > 1.2× target due to network jitter, we'll run a sticky-routing experiment to evaluate improvement.

—Monica
